item.title: Generative AI and New Methods of Inquiry in Information Systems Research
item.content:encoded:
Ahmed Abbasi, University of Notre Dame

Martin Bichler, Technical University of Munich

Ram Gopal, University of Warwick

Elena Karahanna, University of Georgia

Suprateek Sarker, University of Virginia

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping not only organizations, markets, and technologies, but also the practice of scientific research itself. Large language models, multimodal foundation models, and increasingly agentic AI systems now participate in activities such as literature discovery, theorizing, data analysis, simulation, coding, and writing.

This Special Issue seeks papers that push the boundaries of what can be achieved through innovative, rigorous, and responsible use of Generative AI in the information systems research process. Rather than focusing on GenAI solely as an object of empirical study, the SI emphasizes GenAI as a research collaborator, instrument, and infrastructure.

The ambition of the SI is twofold: to publish a small number of exemplary papers that demonstrate novel research capabilities enabled by GenAI, and to advance shared principles, frameworks, and practices that will shape how information systems research is conducted and reported in an era of human–AI collaboration.

Appel publié par Information Systems Research. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Hybrid human–AI workflows for coding, classification, or sensemaking
  • GenAI-supported measurement development, construct validation, or scale refinement
  • GenAI-supported survey design, sampling, and survey administration
  • GenAI-supported experimental design, treatment generation, and implementation
  • GenAI-supported computational theory construction
  • Simulation, agent-based modeling, or scenario generation
  • GenAI-enabled qualitative analysis, theory building, or inductive discovery
  • GenAI-assisted econometric modeling, estimation, or robustness analysis
  • AI-supported proof search, counterexample generation, or equilibrium exploration
  • Discovery or validation of analytical models using generative simulation
  • GenAI-assisted testing of operational utility and/or design validity
  • Design and evaluation of GenAI-based tools for IS research
  • Reproducible pipelines, benchmarks, and evaluation harnesses
  • Systems supporting transparency, provenance, and verification

Timeline

  • September 7, 2026: Submission deadline
  • November 20, 2026: First-round decisions
  • December 13, 2026: ICIS Workshop
  • January 15, 2027: Optional online workshop
  • February 15, 2027: Final version submitted
  • May 1, 2027: Final decisions

item.title: Back to basics in R&D Management: Rediscovering the importance of company case studies
item.content:encoded:
This special issue aims to reverse the trend of declining case study research, rediscovering and reaffirming the value of case studies on the organization and management of R&D to capture the nuances of this specific function in organizational settings and to provide actionable insights for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers. By bringing practical perspectives back to the forefront with a focus on single and multiple case studies, the special issue aims to reconnect theoretical developments with the direct experiences of companies managing innovation on the ground.

Appel publié par R and D Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Case studies on the organization and management of R&D
  • Single and multiple case studies of R&D management
  • Practical perspectives on managing innovation in organizational settings
  • Reconnecting theory with company experiences in R&D management
  • Nuances of R&D function in organizational contexts

Timeline

  • November 1, 2026: Submission window opens

item.title: Capturing Value in the Digital Era: Organizing for Innovation Protection and Information Security
item.content:encoded:
R&D Management has a rich publication history in research on appropriability, intellectual capital and capturing value from innovation. This special issue seeks to update and extend that tradition by explicitly bringing together two adjacent but typically separated conversations.

The first conversation conceptualizes protection of innovation in relation to appropriability mechanisms such as patents, trade secrecy, licensing, contracting, complementary assets, and ecosystem governance to investigate value capture potential.

The second conversation - so far mainly happening in information systems and engineering journals - conceptualizes protection of innovation as information security, such as the protection of R&D artifacts, risks of leakage and theft, industrial espionage, and applications of organizational secrecy for R&D purposes.

Appel publié par R and D Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Appropriability mechanisms such as patents, trade secrecy, licensing, contracting, complementary assets, and ecosystem governance
  • Value capture potential from innovation
  • Protection of R&D artifacts
  • Risks of leakage and theft in innovation
  • Industrial espionage
  • Organizational secrecy for R&D purposes
  • Information security in innovation management
  • Intellectual capital and capturing value from innovation

Timeline

  • February 1, 2027: Submissions open
  • April 30, 2027: Submission deadline

item.title: The Non-Human Innovator: Agentic AI, Physical AI, and the Transformation of R&D Management
item.content:encoded:
This Special Issue is explicitly positioned around a question that existing work on AI-enabled knowledge search, collaboration management, and general AI governance has not yet answered: what happens when AI ceases to be a mere instrument and becomes an agent of innovation? This distinction — between AI-as-tool and AI-as-innovator — defines the conceptual boundary of our four research themes, which address the optimal human–AI division of innovative labour, the architecture of autonomously populated innovation ecosystems, the reimagination of absorptive capacity for an agentic era, and the fundamental challenges to IP posed by non-human inventorship.

Appel publié par R and D Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Optimal human-AI division of innovative labour
  • Architecture of autonomously populated innovation ecosystems
  • Reimagination of absorptive capacity for an agentic era
  • Fundamental challenges to intellectual property posed by non-human inventorship

Timeline

  • June 30, 2027: Deadline for submissions

item.title: Bridging digitalisation, sustainability, and resilience through systems thinking tools: Integrated perspectives and collaborative practices for SMEs
item.content:encoded:
Rui Torres de Oliveira, Deakin University

Agnes Toth-Peter, University of Queensland

Martie-Louise Verreynne, University of Queensland

David Audretsch, Indiana University

Domenico Dentoni, MBS School of Business

Andrea Chiarini, University of Verona

The 21st century presents a range of complex and interdependent challenges, including climate change, resource depletion, economic inequality, and technological disruptions. These so-called wicked problems demand a paradigm shift in our approach to problem-solving. Addressing such challenges requires multi-stakeholder partnerships and holistic, systems-level approaches that transcend traditional, siloed methodologies. Systems thinking, a powerful tool for understanding complexity and interconnections, offers a pathway to sustainable solutions.

Appel publié par Journal of Small Business Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Applications of systems thinking tools, such as causal loop diagrams (CLDs), system archetypes, and system dynamics modeling, in addressing sustainability challenges
  • Development and validation of systems-level frameworks and methodologies for sustainable development
  • Case studies demonstrating the impact of systems thinking on real-world sustainability and/or digitalisation initiatives
  • Use of group model building and participatory system dynamics to support interdisciplinary and ecosystem solutions
  • Exploration of system archetypes and system dynamics models to identify leverage points for driving transformational change and to investigate levers in cross-boundary settings
  • The role of digital technologies, including IoT, AI, big data, and blockchain, in enabling systems-level insights and solutions in the circular economy and sustainability initiatives
  • Integration of digitalisation with circular economy strategies and Industry 5.0 principles and potentials
  • Innovative approaches to digital transformation that promote sustainable development
  • Cross-sectoral and interdisciplinary research to foster collaboration in bridging sustainability and digitalisation, using systems thinking
  • The role of ecosystems in sustainable business models and the boundaries of entrepreneurial ecosystems
  • Methodologies for recognising, assessing and addressing the interconnectedness of environmental, economic, and social systems
  • Open innovation in new sustainable businesses, considering distinct institutional contexts and economic systems, such as emerging and developed economies

Timeline

  • October 1, 2026: Rolling submissions begin
  • May 31, 2027: Manuscript deadline for rolling submissions

item.title: Reimagining Small Business Futures - AI, Inclusion, and Territorial Innovation
item.content:encoded:
Nicola Cucari, Sapienza University of Rome

Guanglei Zhang, Wuhan University of Technology

Jintao Lu, Shanxi University of Electronic Science and Technology

Hua Fan, Shanghai International Studies University

Eric Liguori, Florida State University

The global innovation landscape is undergoing a profound restructuring. Collaboration among geographically distributed innovation ecosystems is intensifying. At the same time, the rapid advancement and diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping the dynamics of global industrial competition. New innovation hubs are emerging across the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, and several emerging economies. In parallel, digital technologies, platformization, and the decentralization of computing power are reducing traditional geographical and scale barriers. As a result, the conditions for competition and innovation are being fundamentally redefined. In this context, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are no longer structurally disadvantaged. Instead, they can increasingly act as agile and innovation-driven players within global value chains.

Appel publié par Journal of Small Business Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

item.title: Artificial Intelligence–Enabled Production Systems: Empirical Evidence, Implementation Pipelines, and Industrial Applications
item.content:encoded:
Ruoqi Geng, Cardiff University

Di Li, Warwick University

Yang Cheng, Aalborg University

Artificial intelligence is rapidly moving from a standalone analytics tool to an operational capability that reshapes how production systems are planned, controlled, and improved in real time. In production contexts, AI can be understood as digital technologies performing tasks and decisions traditionally associated with human intelligence. Recent operations and production research highlights that AI's operational value increasingly depends on data availability, interoperability, and sharing across heterogeneous systems, enabling AI to sense, learn, and act within production environments rather than merely supporting off-line analysis.

Appel publié par Production Planning & Control. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • AI-Augmented Production Planning and Control: predictive and prescriptive analytics for production planning, sequencing, scheduling, and dispatching; reinforcement learning and autonomous decision-making for factory operations; AI-supported capacity management and workflow optimisation
  • Business–AI Alignment and AI Readiness Pipeline for Production Systems: translation of production decisions into AI use cases and data requirements; data governance, quality monitoring, preparation, cleaning, and integration; measures of AI readiness
  • AI-enabled Quality and Process Control: machine learning and deep learning for defect detection and predictive quality control; sensor data and image analytics for automated inspection; AI-driven adaptive process regulation
  • Agentic and Workflow-Oriented Deployment in Production: AI-enabled workflows connecting data preparation to production decisions; natural-language interfaces and AI-assisted decision support; production agents operationalising decision guidance
  • AI-Enabled Cyber–Physical Production Systems and Digital Twins: intelligent digital twins for real-time optimisation; hybrid physics–AI approaches; continuous learning and data synchronisation; edge AI for decentralised decision-making; human–robot collaboration
  • AI and Additive Manufacturing: generative design and topology optimisation; AI-enabled defect prediction and build-path optimisation; distributed AM network coordination; end-user leverage of AI for customisation
  • AI and Blockchain for Production Systems: AI-enhanced traceability and secure data sharing; AI-blockchain integration for auditability and transparency; smart contracts in production automation
  • Human–AI Interaction and Organisational Transformation: human-in-the-loop AI and operator–AI collaboration; organisational readiness and capability development; explainability, trust, transparency, and governance mechanisms
  • Empirical Innovations in Data, Measurement, and Evaluation: field experiments, industry datasets, IoT streams, and digital twin logs; measurable improvements in productivity, quality, flexibility, and decision accuracy
  • Extended Production Contexts: AI in warehousing and fulfilment operations; AI-enabled autonomous mobile robots; real-time slotting and vision systems for object recognition

item.title: Enhancing Transparency and Replicability in Entrepreneurship Research with Preregistrations, Registered Reports, and Registered Revisions
item.content:encoded:
Katharina Fellnhofer, ETH Zurich

Karl Wennberg, Stockholm School of Economics

Thomas H. Allison, Texas Christian University

Pia Arenius, Emlyon Business School

Moren Lévesque, York University

J. Jeffrey Gish, Syracuse University

Jeffrey M. Pollack, NC State University

Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice (ETP) is committed to working alongside entrepreneurship scholars to advance transparency, replicability, credibility, and rigor in empirical research. This special issue encourages authors to preregister research plans, submit empirical studies as Registered Reports — papers that receive editorial decisions before empirical results are known — and engage with ETP's contemporary Registered Revision process. ETP is pleased to announce a virtual special issue featuring Registered Reports, supporting its longstanding dedication to methodological innovation.

A growing body of literature spanning multiple disciplines including entrepreneurship explores the importance of credibility and replicability in scientific inquiry and how scientific rigor can be improved. This call for papers reinforces these efforts in entrepreneurship research by specifically advocating for scholars to submit studies as Registered Reports. The Registered Report format has evolved rapidly from a niche innovation to a widely adopted practice. Since the introduction of the Registered Report format in 2013, more than 300 journals have embraced the approach.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Entrepreneurship Ex Machina: Transformative Artificial Intelligence for Theory and Practice
item.content:encoded:
Martin Obschonka, University of Amsterdam

Moren Lévesque, York University

Frédéric Ooms, HEC Liège

Jeffrey M. Pollack, NC State University

Denis A. Grégoire, HEC Montréal

Tara S. Behrend, Michigan State University

Boris Nikolaev, Colorado State University

Transformative Artificial Intelligence (AI) — that is, the use of AI tools that have such inherent capabilities that they could induce societal transitions similar to that of the agricultural or industrial revolutions — has become an omnipresent topic of interest. Because these tools offer order-of-magnitude efficiency improvements over prior ways of performing various human tasks, important research opportunities arise for better understanding their transformative impact.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Theorizing on algorithmic entrepreneurship
  • Mechanisms of external enablement of entrepreneurship via AI (e.g., generative AI)
  • Can AI help reduce the destructive aspects of entrepreneurship (e.g., societal and personal costs)?
  • Can AI create resource abundance, overcoming typical entrepreneurial resource scarcity and challenging leading startup methods (e.g., effectuation/bricolage, bootstrapping, lean startup)?
  • Do classic research findings and theories (e.g., on the role of knowledge and human and social capital in entrepreneurship) still hold in the new AI era?
  • How can AI impact entrepreneurial finance (e.g., AI-powered financial planning for entrepreneurs, VC investment portfolio management and decisions) and resource acquisition (e.g., entrepreneurs' pitch preparation, investors' due diligence, etc.)?
  • Does AI change the age curve associated with entrepreneurship (does it replace the advantage of industry experience, and do we therefore see an AI-empowered rise of youth entrepreneurs)?
  • How can AI contribute to equality and diversity (e.g., neurodiversity, closing the gender gap)?
  • Ethical and legal issues of algorithmic entrepreneurship and AI-supported research
  • How can AI support entrepreneurs' cognition, decision making, and psychological well-being?

item.title: Organizing Sustainably with Nature in the Global South
item.content:encoded:
Simone Barakat, Fundação Getulio Vargas

Maria Ehrnström-Fuentes, Hanken School of Economics

Seray Ergene, University of Rhode Island

Steffen Farny, Leuphana University Luneburg

Judy Muthuri, University of the West Indies

Contemporary sustainability challenges increasingly foreground organizations as embedded within complex social-ecological systems rather than operating independently from them. While ecological degradation and resource constraints affect organizations worldwide, these challenges are more immediate and structurally embedded in the operating environments of the Global South. These challenges are not just a background context to which organizations must adapt but an outcome of long-standing patterns of extraction, uneven development, and entrenched social inequalities that continue to shape what sustainability can mean in practice.

Appel publié par Organization & Environment. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Organizing for Environmental Sustainability across Communities and Regions - How do communities and organizations work together to govern natural resources and shared ecological commons?
  • How do sustainability standards, certifications, and supply-chain rules influence organizational practices across regions?
  • How do organizations manage environmental interdependencies across local and global contexts?
  • What challenges arise when local ecological priorities clash with global market or regulatory pressures, and how do organizations deal with these challenges in practice?
  • Organizing with Nature from a Global South perspective - How do organizations in the Global South manage their activities within the carrying ecological capacity of the planet (i.e., planetary boundaries), particularly under conditions of resource constraints and institutional fragility?
  • How do organizations in the Global South engage with degrowth, sufficiency, circular, or regenerative practices?
  • What tensions do organizations in the Global South face between economic survival and ecological realities, and how do they navigate these circumstances in practice?
  • How organizations in the Global South conceptualize and manage their embeddedness within social–ecological systems and attempt to develop a regenerative dynamic with nature?
  • Power, Inequality, and the Governance of Nature - What are the sources of environmental injustices currently in the global South? How are they experienced? What are some resistances to these injustices, and how do they unfold? What are some policy mechanisms (if any) to address these injustices?
  • How do power asymmetries manifest in sustainability governance and transnational regulations?
  • How do corporations influence environmental policy and access to natural resources?
  • How do resistance and counter-organizing emerge around contested environmental futures?
  • Stakeholders and Environmental Sustainability from a Global South Perspective - How do organizations in the Global South engage with stakeholders in relation to environmental sustainability?
  • How are the interests of diverse stakeholders, such as communities, governments, NGOs, and other stakeholders, navigated around environmental risks and resource use?
  • How do stakeholder relationships influence organizational decisions and practices related to environmental sustainability?
  • How do power asymmetries and dependency relations among stakeholders shape environmental outcomes and organizing processes?

item.title: Reconceptualizing Careers in Disruptive Times
item.content:encoded:
Jos Akkermans, VU University

David G. Collings, Trinity College Dublin

Mila Lazarova, Simon Fraser University

Jennifer Tosti-Kharas, Babson College

Career theory has evolved over recent decades. Classic career theories were grounded in relatively stable organizational contexts with hierarchical career paths and a relatively stable external context. In the 1990s, there was increasing recognition of the emergence of more flexible, dynamic careers, driven by technological disruption, demographic shifts, and the rise of non-traditional work and career paths. This development is still often referred to as the 'new career' paradigm. Career theories (e.g., boundaryless career theory, protean career theory, and social cognitive career theory) and concepts (e.g., career orientations, career competencies, and career self-management) within that paradigm primarily emphasize theorizing how individuals can take charge and successfully navigate volatile career paths.

Appel publié par Organizational Psychology Review. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do ongoing social, technological, and geopolitical disruptions challenge existing assumptions embedded in dominant career theories?
  • How can new conceptual models better account for the relational and contextual aspects of career development in uncertain and changing environments?
  • How should we reconceptualize concepts such as career competencies and employability in labor markets characterized by volatility, automation, and shifting skill demands?
  • How can careers be reconceptualized in non-traditional work, including the gig economy, internal job deconstruction, and entrepreneurship?
  • How do new forms of digital, hybrid, or platform-mediated work reshape notions of career identity, career success, and career self-management?
  • What role does AI, including agentic AI, and the potential role of AI agents as co-workers play in how individuals' careers evolve?
  • How can career theories and concepts be adapted or renewed to capture the career experiences of underrepresented and marginalized groups?
  • How do organizational, institutional, and labor market structures shape individuals' capacity to construct meaningful and sustainable career paths during times of disruption?
  • How do global mobility patterns, migration, and geopolitical conflict reshape traditional narratives of career progression and mobility?
  • What new methodological or conceptual tools are needed to theorize non-linear, fragmented, or cyclical career patterns that increasingly deviate from traditional career models?

Timeline

item.title: Time in Entrepreneurship: New Perspectives and Approaches
item.content:encoded:
Ludvig Levasseur, Indian Institute of Management Bangalore

Moren Lévesque, York University

Paul Spee, University of Queensland

Ute Stephan, King's College London

Matthew Wood, University of Oklahoma

This special issue seeks manuscripts advancing our understanding of time in entrepreneurship. Research on the duration, pace, timing, and speed of action calibration in entrepreneurial processes such as opportunity realization are key examples of the role temporal dynamics play in entrepreneurship. Time is equally critical when examining decisions about the timing of growth while managing external events and shocks alongside slowly or rapidly evolving industry trends and customer preferences. Further lines of inquiry concern the pace, timing, and speed of exit decisions, or decisions to pursue venturing activities over time. Entrepreneurs' subjective perceptions of time, and their own and their stakeholders' orientations towards the short- vs. long-term, the past, present or future shape how they navigate entrepreneurship.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do objective dimensions such as duration, pace, timing, speed, and window of opportunity impact the entrepreneurship process?
  • How do they shape links between entrepreneurs' subjective time perspective, their biological time (chronotype), and cognitive processes related to information scanning and learning?
  • How do entrepreneurs' subjective time perspectives relate to their cognitions including information scanning and search, entrepreneurial learning, information associations and connections, and opportunity evaluation and judgment?
  • How do time perspectives relate to informal investors' and venture capitalists' decision to provide funding?
  • How do investors' time perspectives shape who they invest in, and the timing and size of their investments?
  • With what pace and speed do failure consequences vary with institutional and cultural contexts?
  • How does the timing of these consequences vary across groups of entrepreneurs including minoritized groups and differently abled entrepreneurs?
  • When and how does time perspective lead to unhealthy persistence in entrepreneurship and undermine well-being?
  • How do entrepreneurs' perception of time and the temporal development of the business impact venture emergence, business sustainability, and social entrepreneurship?
  • Do we see variations in temporal profiles and differences across industries and cultures?
  • How do the pacing of external events and entrepreneurs' own time perspective relate to how they manage equity, diversity, decolonization, and inclusion within their ventures?

item.title: Artificial Intelligence, Business, and Epochal Change
item.content:encoded:
Glen Whelan, ESG UQÀM

Gabriel Weber, ESSCA School of Management

Yann Truong, ESSCA School of Management

Ongoing developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI) indicate that machine learning technologies will not simply match, but will potentially significantly surpass, a wide range of human cognitive abilities. Given this trend, there is reason to believe that AI could threaten humanity's hegemonic, agentic, positioning and that it could be a driver of civilizational, epochal change.

Business actors occupy a unique dual-position within this context. First, as leading architects of AI development, high-tech corporations are rebuilding the organizational structures, labour markets, and human-machinic assemblages that will define social existence for decades to come by impacting upon such fundamental concerns as democracy, peace, and human flourishing. Second, the institution of business and markets as a whole will also find itself the subject of transformative forces that it cannot control despite the fact that certain actors therewithin – such as high-tech corporations – have given rise to them.

Appel publié par Business & Society. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: AI-Enabled Experience Innovation
item.content:encoded:
Bernd Schmitt, Columbia University

Ming-Hui Huang, National Taiwan University

Sanjay Sood, University of California, Los Angeles

Shuyi Hao, ICN Business School

AI is innovating how service experiences can be designed, curated, and delivered. Service that emphasizes experiential components, such as sensory, affective, cognitive, behavioral and social elements, are considered experiential service. Customer experience is multidimensional across multiple touchpoints, unfolds over the customer journey, can be enabled by various AI technologies, and can establish emotional connections with customers.

This special issue seeks to advance our understanding of how AI can enable experience innovation. By enabling personalization, adaptive interaction, and multisensory engagement, AI allows service providers to create new, innovative experiences and enables customers to participate in journeys that evolve dynamically with their needs and preferences. For examples, augmented and virtual reality technologies (AR/VR) are used in retailing to innovate experiences; extended-reality technologies (XR) are used to bring static museum exhibitions to life, mixed-reality technologies (MR) are used to blend real and virtual skill development, and AI technologies are used to enhance sports or entertainment experiences through digital images and surround sound.

Appel publié par Journal of Service Research. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do AI technologies (e.g., generative AI, agentic AI, AR, VR, XR, MR) innovate service experiences, and what design principles help service providers create engaging and meaningful experiences?
  • How should AI-enabled experiences be orchestrated across physical, digital, and extended-reality touchpoints throughout the service journey?
  • How can service providers create and scale AI-enabled experience innovations for human customers, hybrid human-AI customers, or autonomous AI customers to generate favorable outcomes for customers, providers, and ecosystems?
  • What new experiential consequences and innovation outcomes arise from AI, and how can they be conceptualized, measured, and managed over time?
  • What ethical, societal, or governance challenges arise and how can AI-enabled experience innovation be designed, governed, and managed responsibly?

item.content:encoded:
Jay Joseph, American University of Beirut

Jennifer Oetzel, American University

Angelika Rettberg, Universidad de los Andes

Global peace is needed now more than ever, yet "peace" still fails to feature in mainstream business and society debates. For over 20 years, "business and peace" has led this debate in business and management studies. Business and peace has generated a broad array of research studies that link business activity to peacebuilding; however, the high volume of descriptive, case-based, and practice-based research in the field, combined with the growing number of parallel contributions to conflict and peace-related topics in general management studies, presents challenges for moving a coherent debate on peace and business forward.

item.title: The Science of Group Meetings
item.content:encoded:
Joseph A. Allen, University of Utah

Nale Lehmann-Willenbrock, University of Hamburg

Meetings remain one of the most pervasive features of organizational life, serving as a critical venue for communication, collaboration, decision-making, and sensemaking in groups and teams. Yet, despite their ubiquity, meetings continue to spark debate over their effectiveness, efficiency, and impact on individuals, teams, and organizations. Moreover, the nature of group and team meetings in organizations is subject to ongoing change, with respect to meeting formats, purposes, and functions.

The aim of this Special Issue is to move forward and examine new perspectives on meetings in contemporary organizational life. We are interested in interdisciplinary and cross-disciplinary submissions that advance the meeting science literature, with a focus on empirical insights into group and team meetings. Both field studies and laboratory research methodology can contribute such insights. However, no studies based on individual-level, self-report, cross-sectional data unless substantiated by additional data will be considered.

Appel publié par Small Group Research. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Advances in meeting design and structuration in face-to-face, virtual, or hybrid group meetings
  • Effective meeting leadership and facilitation in various meeting formats
  • Psychological safety, inclusion, and equity in meetings
  • Meeting participation and engagement (including "pretend participation" or the act of appearing to participate in a meeting without actually contributing meaningfully to the group's goals)
  • Pre-meeting and post-meeting tasks
  • Decision-making and problem-solving in meetings
  • Linking within-meeting dynamics to relevant meeting experiences at the individual and/or team level (e.g., satisfaction, effectiveness, well-being, creativity)
  • Technology and meetings (e.g., AI applications in hybrid and virtual formats)
  • Meeting overload, fatigue, and recovery
  • Emotional dynamics and surface/deep acting in meetings
  • Diversity, identity, and power in meeting interactions
  • Training and interventions for effective meetings
  • Measurement and assessment of meeting quality and effectiveness

item.title: Collective actorhood and organizationality: Recalibrating responsibility in business-society relations
item.content:encoded:
Dennis Schoeneborn, Copenhagen Business School

Héloïse Berkowitz, CNRS, Aix Marseille University

Leonhard Dobusch, University of Innsbruck

Frank de Bakker, IÉSEG School of Management

Consuelo Vásquez, Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM)

Over the past decades, the relations between business and society have fundamentally changed. We are entering an age of digital futures with artificial intelligence taking over more and more human tasks at rapid speed, as well as broken futures with accelerating dynamics of climate change, in which the survival of humankind will depend on our ability to organize in collective ways and imagine alternatives to tackle such complex social problems, amidst growing inequalities and ecological destruction on a planetary scale.

Appel publié par Business & Society. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How is collective actorhood performed and organized?
  • Is a legal status/legal person needed to accomplish collective actorhood?
  • Why and how do actors strategically downplay or amplify collective actorhood? How do these strategic efforts affect responsibility attributions?
  • What are the implications and limitations of collective actorhood for reenvisioning the business-society relationship and offer alternative solutions in crises of civilization?
  • Where and how does actorhood emerge? How do institutional contexts affect actorhood?
  • How does actorhood evolve over time or space, and how do organizations transition between different degrees of organizationality?
  • Can social collectives be perpetuated and maintained even with a low degree of organizationality – or do they feel pressures either to be dissolved or evolve toward higher degrees of organizationality eventually?
  • How to explain asymmetric dynamics between the organized (e.g., established formal organizations; high degree of organizationality) and the (rather) unorganized as their counterparts (e.g., social media firestorm; low degree of organizationality)?
  • What can we learn from alternative forms of organizing, including those in marginalized settings?
  • How is collective actorhood conceptualized in the various geographies, including the Global South? How does this translate, circulate, and adapt across geographies?
  • What are the contributions of other collective notions stemming from indigenous cosmovisions and decolonial approaches?
  • How does actorhood affect the interactions between organizations from different domains (for profit and non-profit, scientific organizations, public actors, etc.)?
  • When does collective actorhood create relations of domination and exploitation?
  • At what point does collective actorhood become constitutive of societal problems and crises (incl. fascism, techno-feudalism, etc.) – rather than a solution for addressing them?
  • How does actorhood (or the lack of) affect the relationship between privileged and marginal communities?
  • Can living (forests, rivers, soils) and non-living (algorithms, technologies) entities be attributed actorhood and be held accountable? How does it differ from 'human' organizing?
  • How can alternative ontologies help inform this analysis?
  • How can a gradual understanding of organization help us to understand variations in the degree of organizational actorhood and responsibility attributions in the relations between businesses and society?
  • What are the parameters of organizationality required for a responsible collective actorhood?
  • How can alternative ontologies, cosmovisions, and organizing experiences inform this critical reflection?
  • How to better account for situations in which marginalized actors are forced into fluid and precarious ways of organizing and/or have no choice to lessen the degree of organizationality to cope or survive?

item.title: Corporate Social Responsibility in Times of Societal Polarization, Politicization, and Securitization
item.content:encoded:
Dorothee Maria Winkler, Bern University of Applied Sciences

David Risi, Bern University of Applied Sciences

Christopher Wickert, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

Onna Malou van den Broek, Copenhagen Business School

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has a long and influential history as one of the dominant paradigms in managing the business-society interface. For years, CSR has served as the normative and strategic blueprint for companies in managing growing societal expectations such as climate change, corruption, and inequality, fundamentally shaping corporate behavior across sustainability, ethics, and stakeholder engagement. Over the past decade, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria seemed to be moving from the periphery to the center of attention for companies, and the formalization and legalization of CSR-related criteria have reinforced the importance of corporate responsibility and consolidated its position as a central area of concern for business firms.

Appel publié par Business & Society. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • What responsibilities do firms assume when navigating heightened political and societal tensions?
  • What does "responsible" corporate behavior mean in today's polarized global political economy?
  • How is CSR evolving to address the complex moral and strategic challenges of an increasingly divided world?
  • Do corporations counter populist and illiberal politics, or primarily align with dominant power structures?
  • How do firms recalibrate ESG and CSR commitments while maintaining legitimacy across diverse stakeholders?
  • Which role does CSR play in specific industries such as defense industrial complex, including defense-focused tech firms?
  • To what extent has CSR enabled corporate political activity (CPA) that influences democratic governance in ways that advance corporate interests?
  • How do new forms of "reverse CSR" or politically adaptive responsibility emerge?
  • How does the geographical context influence the conceptualization of CSR?
  • Is CSR diffusing from autocratic to democratic contexts as a tool of political signaling rather than social progress?
  • How do the underlying philosophical and epistemological assumptions of CSR differ across contexts?
  • How can established theoretical perspectives account for geopolitically fragmented CSR models?
  • How can nationalistic or "Western populist" CSR be conceptualized in a priori democratic contexts?
  • What theoretical frameworks need to be developed to account for the instrumentalization of CSR for national and geopolitical purposes?
  • Which role does CSR play in contexts of violent conflict?
  • How do security demands shape CSR's definition and scope?
  • What new priorities emerge when CSR is applied in the defense industry, particularly regarding process vs. product dimensions?
  • How do polarization, politicization, and securitization collectively shape CSR trajectories, and what role do businesses, governments, and other stakeholders play?
  • How do businesses weigh and prioritize imperatives posed by polarization, politicization, and securitization, and how does this influence their CSR agendas?
  • How do businesses recalibrate their CSR strategies to account for new and competing societal priorities?
  • How do governments integrate these dynamics when devising or revising CSR regulations?
  • Do we see emerging surveillance states arising from mutually beneficial collaborations between the defense-industrial complex (including tech firms) and governments?
  • Do we observe any sidelining or dismantling of international institutions and cooperation structures established after the Second World War?
  • How do societal stakeholders navigate this nexus when formulating expectations towards businesses and exerting pressure?

item.title: Family Firms as Context for Organizational Behavior Processes
item.content:encoded:
Melanie De Ruiter, Nyenrode Business University

Benjamin D. McLarty, Louisiana Tech University

Denise M. Rousseau, Carnegie Mellon University

James M. Vardaman, Memphis University

Despite calls to consider context in Organizational Behavior (OB) and management research, the broader OB and management literature has largely ignored family firms and the experiences and employment dynamics of their employees. OB research samples often are drawn without considering the nature of the settings involved or any potential impact on the variables of interest. Since family firms are a common type of business, ranging from sixty-five to ninety percent worldwide, samples in many OB and management studies likely conflate respondents from family and non-family firms. Such conflation can mask differences in behavioral processes that can result in erroneous inferences.

Treatment of family/non-family business as a dichotomous moderator only allows general differences to be noted without theoretically comparing psychological processes at the individual, team, and organizational levels. Moreover, since there is considerable heterogeneity within family firms, grouping employees working in different family firms together will likely forego important across family firm contextual differences in OB processes. Most studies in family firm research have been described as 'context-less'.

Appel publié par Group & Organization Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Development and validation of measurement instruments (including assessment of measurement invariance) that allow a more generic assessment of contextual effects often put forward in family firm research (e.g., socioemotional wealth) to help theorize and understand similarities and differences in OB processes between family and non-family firms, and within family firms
  • Explicit tests of theories of context (e.g., trait activation theory; situation strength theory) to explain differences in relationships between personality traits and employee outcomes between family and non-family firms and within different types of family firms (e.g., enhanced understanding of family firm context as a driver for personality activation and impact on workplace performance and behaviors)
  • Development and validation of personality measurement instruments specific to the context of family for use in family firms, and meaningful contextual comparisons across family firms (including assessment of measurement invariance)
  • Enhanced theoretical understanding of how bifurcation bias based on family firm context as a potential motivational force for driving employee attitudes and behaviors
  • Multilevel research to better understand how the family firm context affects the extent to which leadership styles may (or may not) trickle down from family executives to family and non-family managers and in turn affect non-family employee outcomes in different types of family firms
  • An exploration of how critical events within the family firm context and family/non-family member dynamics shape employee and non-family manager perceptions and evaluations of their employment relationship with the family firm

item.title: Imagining Post-Growth
item.content:encoded:
Fred Basso, London School of Economics and Political Science

Nil Özçağlar-Toulouse, Université de Lille

Julien Troiville, ESG Université du Québec À Montréal

Humanity has entered a critical period to limit catastrophic climate change. Global warming is primarily due to human activity, and efforts to remain below 1.5°C have been insufficient. More than ever, marketing must act to encourage behaviors and choices compatible with truly sustainable lifestyles. Post-growth has emerged as a major research topic, carried by environmental and economic sciences as well as social sciences such as history, sociology and political science. It challenges the dependence of our societies on economic growth, the central place accorded to consumption-based well-being, and the supposed link between prosperity and productivism.

Interest in post-growth is reflected in the proliferation of articles in renowned scientific journals, the release of documentaries, and the creation of research centers dedicated to this topic. Management sciences are also engaged, as evidenced by calls for contributions for special issues devoted to post-growth or edited works. This special issue aims to advance theory and practice by exploring how researchers, consumers and practitioners implement strategies to prepare for post-growth.

Appel publié par Recherche et Applications en Marketing (French Edition). Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How marketing can challenge the status quo: Creating new desires vs. responding to individual needs; Marketing as a political choice reinforcing capitalism; Critical reflection on critical marketing; Ethical marketing practices and their relationship to the economic system; Individual vs. systemic responsibility in consumer behavior (I-frame vs. S-frame); Nudging and boosting as neoliberal strategies
  • How marketing can engage in degrowth practices: Transformative practices for degrowth strategies; Role of marketing experts in post-growth economic transitions; Reinventing marketing practices, training and education; Overcoming tensions within the economy; Internal growth transformations and moving away from materialism; Conceptual clarification of degrowth, post-growth, demarketing, regenerative economy, donut economy, ecosocial marketing, decarbonized marketing
  • How a post-growth economy can be sustained: Transitioning from unlimited desires to meeting human needs; Consumption corridors and sufficient consumption; Marketing roles and practices to maintain in post-growth society; Reduced working time and prefigurative organizations; Moving beyond technological utopias to social utopias; Public policies for degrowth transitions; Economic development equity between Global North and South; Escaping extractivism and postcolonial systems

  • Invalid DateTime: Special issue publication online
  • January 15, 2027: Full paper submission deadline

item.title: Immanent Critique in Management Learning and Education: Organizational Contradictions, Emancipatory Possibilities, and Institutional Transformation
item.content:encoded:
Torkild Thanem, Stockholm University

Shoaib Ul Haq, University of Greenwich

Sara Zaeemdar, Newcastle University

Iain Munro, Newcastle University

Alice Wickström, Aalto University

Farooq Mughal, University of Bath

This special issue addresses an underexplored concern in Management Learning and Education (MLE): the contradictions between the emancipatory ideals espoused by business schools and the institutional, ideological and economic logics they reproduce. Critics have charged MLE with neoliberal, colonial, racist, and sexist practices, which reproduce the harms and injustices of capitalism. However important such work is, these critiques have largely been mounted from a position external to the institutions they target. Less examined is how transformation may be pursued from inside MLE itself, by holding business schools accountable to the very ideals they profess.

Appel publié par Management Learning. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Theoretical contributions developing immanent critique for MLE contexts
  • Scholarship examining how management education's contradictions relate to broader transformations in capitalism, knowledge production, and subjectivity formation
  • Efforts to rework immanent critique through decolonial, indigenous, and/or feminist epistemologies to address its Western/male-dominated philosophical origins
  • Efforts to develop conceptual frameworks for understanding emancipatory learning within constrained institutional contexts
  • Analyses of how business school commitments to sustainability, EDI, or social responsibility play out in curricular design, pedagogical practice, and institutional governance
  • Ethnographic investigations of alternative management education programs that attempt to embody different values while operating within conventional accreditation and funding structures
  • Studies of alternative institutional forms of management learning, such as cooperatives, free universities, worker-owned schools, platform-cooperative training programs, indigenous-led and faith-based business education
  • Critical investigations of the effects of the rise of far-right political leaders on progressive initiatives in education, such as EDI initiatives, equal pay and promotions, sustainability and ESG measures, and campus protests
  • Participatory research approaches that engage educators and learners as co-researchers in identifying and addressing educational contradictions
  • Arts-based methods for surfacing and representing the affective dimensions of educational contradictions and their role in reproducing or challenging institutional norms
  • Digital ethnographies examining online management education platforms and their claims versus experiences
  • Studies of the pedagogy of growth taught alongside curricula on planetary boundaries, ecological economics, and post-growth alternatives
  • Analyses of sustainability and ESG modules as moments of managerial absorption rather than ecological reckoning
  • Engagements with climate-justice movements as sources of immanent normative reconstruction inside the business school

item.title: Multinational Enterprises and the Sustainable Development Goals: Evolving Roles, Challenges, and Opportunities Beyond 2030
item.content:encoded:
Huda Khan, University of Aberdeen

Hussain Rammal, Adelaide University

Pervez Ghauri, University of Birmingham

Zaheer Khan, University of Aberdeen

Martin Meyer, University of Vaasa

The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), adopted in 2015, provide a comprehensive global agenda addressing critical social, economic, and environmental challenges, with the target of achieving these goals by 2030. These 17 interconnected goals range from eradicating poverty and ensuring quality education to combating climate change and fostering sustainable economic growth. As the global community works toward this ambitious target, the role of Multinational Enterprises (MNEs) has become increasingly vital. MNEs, with their significant financial resources, innovation capabilities, and extensive global reach, are uniquely positioned to contribute meaningfully to the realization of these global objectives. However, integrating the SDGs into business strategies presents considerable challenges, especially in light of evolving institutional, political, and social dynamics.

Appel publié par Business & Society. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • MNEs' Evolving Role in the SDGs' Agenda: Achievements, Gaps, and Future Directions - How can MNEs evaluate their contributions to the SDGs and adjust their strategies to meet the 2030 targets? What opportunities and challenges will MNEs face post-2030 in continuing to support the SDGs' agenda? How can MNEs address the lagging targets of the SDGs in their operations?
  • Managing ESG Backlash and its impact on MNEs' SDGs' Alignment - How does the ESG backlash impact MNEs' strategies for achieving the SDGs? In what ways do political and institutional pressures shape MNEs' SDG agendas? How can MNEs maintain their commitment to the SDGs amidst the growing scepticism toward ESG?
  • Institutional Dynamics and MNEs' SDGs' Engagement - How do formal and informal institutional logics influence MNEs' strategies for addressing SDGs in different host countries? How do institutional voids in emerging markets shape MNEs' SDG engagement? What roles do institutional actors (governments, NGOs, civil society) play in shaping MNEs' SDG commitments?
  • Business and Society Perspectives on MNEs and SDGs: Bridging IB and B&S Literature - How can IB literature inform B&S's understandings of MNEs' contributions to SDGs? How do MNEs reconcile profit motives with societal goals in their SDGs' strategies? What are the synergies between business model innovation and sustainable development in the context of the SDGs?
  • Leveraging Global Value Chains for Sustainable Development - What practical strategies can MNEs adopt to integrate sustainability into their global value chains to meet SDGs' targets? What are the opportunities for MNEs to collaborate with supply chain partners on SDGs' initiatives? How can knowledge transfer across value chains improve SDGs' outcomes?
  • Organizational Forms and Alliance for SDGs: Bridging IB and BAS Perspectives - How can MNEs and their partners in cross-sector alliances navigate the challenges of aligning values, beliefs, and power dynamics in SDG-driven initiatives? In what ways can partnerships between MNEs, governments, NGOs, and CSOs enhance the achievement of SDGs, particularly in areas such as inclusive development and climate action? What role do MNE headquarters play in supporting subsidiaries and local network partners to integrate global sustainability principles into their operations? How can MNEs collaborate with SMEs to achieve SDGs, and what benefits does this collaboration bring to local communities? How do strategic alliances contribute to the long-term sustainability of SDG initiatives, and what organizational forms are most effective in fostering these collaborations?
  • Micro-foundations of MNEs' Engagement with SDGs: Motivations, Leadership, and Human Capital - How do the personal experiences and values of top management, including the CEO, influence MNEs' strategies for addressing the SDGs? What role does diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) play in shaping top management's engagement with sustainability goals and advancing SDGs? How do leadership styles and top management teams influence employee engagement with SDG initiatives within MNEs? What mechanisms within MNEs' governance structures support or hinder the integration of SDGs into business models, particularly in the areas of poverty eradication, climate action, and social equity? How do individual decision-makers contribute to business model innovations that advance SDGs, and how do these innovations affect the company's long-term sustainability efforts?

Timeline

item.title: Organizing within the Planetary Boundaries
item.content:encoded:
Steve Kennedy, Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University

Brooke Lahneman, Montana State University

Lucrezia Nava, University of Exeter Business School

Amanda Williams, EM Lyon Business School

Scholarship on business sustainability increasingly views organizations as embedded within natural systems, conceptualized through the planetary boundaries framework. The planetary boundary framework defines nine Earth system processes that regulate the planet's stability and resilience and are directly affected by human activity. Alarmingly, seven of these nine boundaries have now been crossed, threatening both natural systems and the economies that depend on them. For business scholarship, this creates an urgent need to understand how organizations can operate and manage within the safe space delineated by planetary boundaries.

Appel publié par Organization & Environment. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How Organizations Integrate the Planetary Boundary Framework into Strategy and Action
  • How organizations leverage planetary boundaries to inform sustainability materiality assessments and sustainability strategies
  • How organizations collectively use planetary boundaries as a basis to inform shared understanding of cross-scale risks across space and time
  • How organizations leverage planetary boundaries to inform risk management approaches
  • How organizations collectively build adaptive capacity for addressing risks and identifying opportunities associated with the planetary boundary framework
  • How organizations utilize planetary boundaries to inform creation of sustainability targets such as SBTi and corporate reporting on environmental impacts
  • How organizations disaggregate planetary boundaries to relevant temporal and spatial scales to inform appropriate action for sustainability
  • How organizations use the planetary boundary framework to shape sectoral and cross-sector collaborations
  • How organizations leverage planetary boundaries as a way to 'unlock' the complexity of the natural environment for business model innovation and/or product design
  • How Organizations Can Operate and Manage within Individual Planetary Boundaries
  • How organizations detect, interpret, and act when a planetary boundary is being approached or transgressed
  • How organizations prepare for risks associated with transgressing the boundaries and innovate to limit planetary boundary transgression
  • How organizations use planetary boundaries for constraint-driven innovation for enhanced practices, processes, business models, and/or collaborations
  • Which processes and practices enable firms to develop proactive and responsive strategies for long-term engagement with a specific planetary boundary
  • How organizations should balance trade-offs between proactive and responsive strategies for a given planetary boundary, given their industry and operating context
  • What roles different stakeholders play in shaping organizational responses to planetary boundary transgressions
  • How organizations can engage with least-studied boundaries such as ocean acidification, biogeochemical flows, atmospheric aerosol loading, stratospheric ozone depletion, and novel entities
  • How to Navigate Interconnections among Planetary Boundaries and with Social Foundations
  • How organizations adapt and innovate strategies, practices, and processes to address interconnections among multiple planetary boundaries
  • How efforts to stay within planetary boundaries can be aligned with advancing key social foundations and UN Sustainable Development Goals
  • How organizations can apply systems-thinking lenses to manage non-linear change, ecosystem risks, and feedback loops across planetary boundaries and/or social systems
  • What governance mechanisms, decision tools, or collaborative arrangements enable organizations and industries to navigate and manage trade-offs across boundaries
  • What role could concepts such as degrowth, carrying capacity, or post-growth business models play in helping organizations remain within interconnected ecological limits
  • How to Develop Alternative Organizational Theories and Practices from Planetary Boundary Biophysical Foundations
  • What innovations in practices, products, and business models emerge when organizational thinking begins with planetary boundaries
  • How integrating the planetary boundary framework can inform or reshape core organizational theories
  • How the planetary boundary framework can inform theory on crisis management and responding to ecosystem shocks such as natural disasters
  • How the planetary boundary framework might advance perspectives on desirable or alternative futures
  • What alternative forms of organizing can be theorized by taking planetary boundaries as foundational
  • How theory on circular and regenerative systems can be informed by considering planetary boundaries

Timeline

  • March 1, 2027: Full manuscript submission deadline

Associate editors

  • Gail Whiteman, University of Exeter Business School

item.title: Our Oceans as a Business-Society Nexus: Advancing the Interplay of Blue Economy, Blue Governance and Blue Justice
item.content:encoded:
Matevž Rašković, Auckland University of Technology

Noemi Sinkovics, Newcastle University

Michelle Voyer, University of Wollongong

Nives Dolšak, University of Washington

Gurmeet Singh, University of the South Pacific

Our oceans make up 70% of our planet, provide transportation for 80% of global goods in volume and ensure the livelihood of over 3 billion people, including many of the global poor. Oceans represent the largest environment-humanity nexus on Earth in environmental, economic, geopolitical and global security, and socio-cultural terms. Yet, as planetary spaces, our oceans are often thought of as separate from humans in a human-nature duality, which limits research on the place-space embeddedness of business in particular environmental materialities like our oceans.

Appel publié par Business & Society. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Business models, value creation, and distribution: How do different ocean-based business models create value, who captures the value and who bears costs across communities, ecosystems, and value/supply chains? What trade-offs and paradoxes emerge between economic growth and social/environmental objectives, and how are they justified, negotiated, or contested by various stakeholders and at different levels? How do firms build, maintain, or lose social licence to operate in ocean- and coast-related activities, and what triggers shifts in legitimacy?
  • Governance, accountability, and power across levels: How do governance arrangements (e.g., local, national, regional, transnational) shape who gets access, who is included/excluded, and how rules are enforced in ocean and coastal settings? When and why do 'good governance' arrangements still produce undesired social outcomes (e.g., exclusion, livelihood disruption), and what mechanisms explain this? How do firms, states, NGOs, and community actors coordinate or compete to frame problems, set standards, and allocate responsibilities and resources?
  • Justice, equity, and lived impacts: How are distributive, procedural, recognitional, and restorative justice concerns expressed in ocean and coastal contexts, and how do they translate into organisational and policy decisions? What forms of inequity arise in practice (e.g., displacement, access restrictions, benefit-sharing), and what interventions have been effective (or ineffective) in redressing them? How do gender, indigeneity, and marginalisation shape participation in governance and benefit-sharing, and what organisational and policy practices enable or constrain inclusion?
  • Ownership, stewardship, and legitimacy: Under what conditions are oceans treated as shared spaces versus commodified resources, and how do firms and states influence these framings? What governance designs or institutional arrangements support credible stewardship (beyond compliance), and how are these maintained or evolve over time? How do alternative understandings of stewardship and collective rights (including Indigenous governance) reshape corporate strategy, accountability, and legitimacy?
  • Risk, contestation, and the 'dark side': How do illegal, informal, or harmful practices (e.g., illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, labour abuses, illicit trade) become embedded in ocean-related industries, and what enables accountability or impunity? How do firms manage reputational, legal, and operational risks linked to ocean-related activities, and when do risk-management approaches conflict with justice and sustainability aims?

Timeline

  • May 1, 2026: Online idea generation workshop
  • August 1, 2026: Online research capacity building workshop for PhD students, early-career scholars and emerging market scholars
  • March 15, 2027: Submission window opens for full papers
  • May 15, 2027: Submission window closes for full papers
  • June 1, 2027: Hybrid PDW for R&R papers at the University of the South Pacific in Fiji
  • November 1, 2027: Online 'Delphi method' workshop for writing a scene-setting future research agenda as part of the Introduction to the Special Issue

item.title: Reexamining and Replicating Foundational Studies in Entrepreneurship Research
item.content:encoded:
Karl Wennberg, Stockholm School of Economics

Jeremy C. Short, University of North Texas

Jeffrey A. Chandler, University of North Texas

Marcus Wolfe, University of North Texas

Sebastian Kruse, RWTH University

Carolin Krieweth, RWTH University

This Special Issue seeks to advance our understanding of replication in entrepreneurship research by encouraging rigorous reexaminations of foundational empirical studies. Replication is essential for cumulative theory development and for establishing confidence in empirical findings. In a dynamic field such as entrepreneurship, where institutional environments, technologies, funding regimes, and societal expectations evolve rapidly, systematic replication is particularly critical to assess whether foundational relationships reflect stable theoretical mechanisms or context-specific patterns.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Influential studies within specific BCERC research tracks highlighted as influential contributions within each track
  • Studies with credible cases for broader influence on entrepreneurship research
  • Identifying boundary conditions and contextual contingencies of established relationships
  • Clarifying inconsistencies or mixed findings in prior research
  • Refining theoretical mechanisms underlying key constructs and relationships
  • Contributing to methodological transparency, rigor, and best practices in replication research
  • Multi-study designs combining exact replication or reanalysis of original data with subsequent empirical generalization or theoretical extension

item.title: Strategy and Aesthetics
item.content:encoded:
René Wiedner, Warwick Business School

Jennifer Whyte, University of Sydney

Saku Mantere, McGill University

Robin Holt, University of Bristol

Marie-Léandre Gomez, ESSEC Business School

There is broad recognition that organizational life cannot be fully understood or managed through rationalist frameworks. Scholars across the social sciences, including human geography and cultural theory, have long acknowledged how sensory experience, emotion, affect and embodied practice shape organization. Strategy studies are also beginning to understand how strategically significant phenomena–organizational routines, capabilities and identity, investment allocation and judgment, leadership, environmental adaptation–refuse to be confined to, and by, rational, logically structured analyses.

There is an aesthetic aspect to all strategy–it is as much vision as it reason; as much inspiration as analysis. Emotions, feelings, intuitions, desires and instincts can all have strategically significant influence. The symbolic and material dimensions of organising, alongside questions of purpose and structure across multiple human practices and fields, are all factors for which a successful strategic design must take account. The discursive, ecological and commercial forces to which organizations are adapting continually are encountered in aesthetic terms.

Appel publié par Strategic Organization. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • The aesthetic qualities of strategy work: combining creative expression with analytical rigor; the coexistence of, and interplay between, poetics and reason
  • Aesthetically-infused experiences such as awe in understanding how strategic organizations resist the disenchantment of strategy work through over-rationalization
  • Studies of strategy confronting cultural landscapes encouraging the production and consumption of styles rather than goods, posing complex strategic identity choices across audiences with different stylistic preferences and evaluation criteria
  • How the strategic organization of affective forces is often caught in a fundamental ambiguity between instrumental organization and unmanageable reorganization of experience
  • Examinations of analogue and digital strategic devices and how these contribute to the performance of strategic styles, including strategy work in boardrooms and informal organizing contexts
  • Investigations of the strategic appropriation of artistic activity and how organizations draw from artistic practices to reinvent themselves and maximize profitability
  • Studies of organizational design and the formation of capabilities and identities that can be structured to elicit strategically significant commitments amongst stakeholders
  • Inquiries of processual forming and formation in strategy, invoking vitalist and new materialist philosophy and questions about organizational forms
  • Engagements with the raw material of strategy in formation, including how information and data have aesthetic forms and dimensions
  • Connecting strategy and temporality through aesthetics, including how strategy forms narrative plots that elicit specific feelings of progression, symbolic and communal attachments, and identities

item.title: The Impact of the Political Environment on Tourism and Hospitality
item.content:encoded:
This special issue seeks to explore the multifaceted ways in which political environments shape and influence the tourism and hospitality sectors. The political context encompasses governmental policies, political stability, regulatory frameworks, international relations, and geopolitical events that directly and indirectly affect tourism flows, hospitality operations, and industry development.

We invite submissions that examine how political factors influence destination competitiveness, tourism demand and supply, hospitality business strategies, employment patterns, and sustainable development in the sector. We particularly welcome research that addresses contemporary political challenges and opportunities in tourism and hospitality.

Contributions may include empirical studies, theoretical frameworks, case studies, and comparative analyses that provide insights into the complex relationships between political environments and tourism and hospitality industries globally.

Appel publié par Journal of Hospitality & Tourism Research. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: The Startup Workforce
item.content:encoded:
James Bort, DePaul University

Veroniek Collewaert, Vlerick Business School

Yuval Engel, University of Amsterdam

Evy Van Lancker, Ghent University

Johan Wiklund, Syracuse University

The startup workforce represents a distinct and consequential stakeholder in entrepreneurship that has been systematically understudied relative to founders and funders. Early insights from the Stanford Project on Emerging Companies revealed how organizational changes within startups disproportionately impacted long-tenured employees. This pioneering work laid the foundation for understanding how startups differ from established firms in their approach to human capital, including fundamental aspects such as compensation, staffing, and performance management.

Contemporary research has deepened our understanding of the unique dynamics between startups and their employees. Whereas early research identified demographic patterns, illustrating that startup employees tend to be younger and risk-tolerant, recent work has uncovered more nuanced dynamics. For example, experienced employees often join startups when they have partners with stable careers, but can also command wage premiums as firms grow. Startup employees are drawn in by passionate founders, opportunities for greater freedom and responsibility, and the potential for significant financial upside.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Employee motivations and retention across venture stages
  • Recruitment, employer branding, and the role of prior affiliations in startup hiring
  • The influence of early employees on organizational culture, routines, and strategic direction
  • Compensation structures, equity arrangements, and evolving psychological contracts
  • Workforce well-being, occupational stress, and founder-employee emotional spillovers
  • The impact of hybrid and remote work on startup employment dynamics
  • The opportunities and adversity of AI in light of startup employment and work ethic, and workforce diversity, inclusion, and the role of HR professionalization in early-stage ventures
  • Worker voice, collective action, and power asymmetries in startups, including unionization, whistleblowing, hustle culture and exploitation, equity and vesting disputes, and the dark side of founder–employee relations
  • The regulatory and institutional environment of startup employment, including non-compete enforcement, worker classification, equity taxation, and visa regimes
  • Non-standard and hybrid labor forms, including contractors, fractional executives, agencies, platform and ghost work, and globally distributed teams
  • Post-startup career trajectories, including employee mobility, alumni networks, and entrepreneurial spawning after exit, acquisition, or failure
  • The scaleup transition and its workforce implications, including when and how a startup workforce ceases to be one and how HR professionalization reshapes the employment relation
  • AI-native ventures as a new organizational form, where a small number of humans operate agentic systems and the category of workforce is itself reconstituted
  • Startup workforces outside North America and Western Europe, including emerging-economy, informal, and cross-border contexts

item.title: Close Relationships in an Interdependent Social World
item.content:encoded:
Sandra Murray, University at Buffalo

Are close relationships in peril? Loneliness is increasing and markers of social engagement (e.g., marriage) are decreasing. This special section hopes to provide insight into this question by tackling the socially nested nature of interdependence itself.

Close relationships with significant others take place in the broader context of family responsibilities, such as those involved in parenting children and caring for aging parents; in the broader context of friendship networks, and broader communities; in the context of sociopolitical pressures, such as economic stress, racism, and political polarization; and in the context of technological changes, such as those posed by the insertion of AI into social life.

Appel publié par Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How contextual or socially nested nature of interdependence shapes close relationship dynamics
  • Relationship dynamics relevant to relationship initiation, maintenance, or dissolution
  • Close relationships in the broader context of family responsibilities (parenting children, caring for aging parents)
  • Close relationships in the broader context of friendship networks and communities
  • Close relationships in the context of sociopolitical pressures (economic stress, racism, political polarization)
  • Close relationships in the context of technological changes (AI insertion into social life)

item.title: Integrative Conceptual Reviews
item.content:encoded:
The Journal of Applied Psychology editorial team invites prospectus submissions that describe a proposed integrative conceptual review (ICR) manuscript on topic areas relevant to human resource management, industrial and organizational psychology, and organizational behavior.

An ICR article should be designed to synthesize relevant literature, identify significant knowledge gaps, highlight potential synergies between disconnected lines of research, extend theoretical development, and propose new directions for research.

Examples of the type of papers that are of interest include articles published in the Annual Review of Psychology, Psychological Science in the Public Interest, the Journal of Management review issue, the Academy of Management Annals, and top-tier handbooks.
